chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Some decisions feel closer to retrieval than to judgment. A deadline can be checked. A score can be looked up. But a candidate can be evaluated, a forecast can be assessed, and a student file can be read in ways that still require interpretation. The chapter's job is to mark that difference without pretending the line is perfectly clean.

That distinction matters because noise belongs where a human scale is still active. If someone has to decide how strong, weak, convincing, risky, or promising a case is, then the output is not simply being fetched from the world. It is being produced through assessment. That is the zone where unstable readings become a serious problem.

The chapter resists two bad simplifications. One says every decision is equally subjective, so the idea of judgment explains nothing. The other says rules remove judgment completely, so noise disappears wherever a standard exists. Neither move is careful enough. Many processes mix rules and interpretation. A rubric can still need reading. A guideline can still need scaling. A category can still need a human assessor to decide how the case fits.

That gray area is the point of the chapter rather than an inconvenience to it. Noise can survive inside respectable institutions because people are often doing more than retrieving a fixed answer even when a rule is present. Whenever interpretation remains active, the judge and the instrument still matter.

This chapter is therefore a scope-setting move. It clarifies where the book's problem really lives so the next chapter can ask how error inside those readings should be measured.
